28698.etyen:
Borrowed from English karate, from Japanese 空手 (karate, “empty hand”). The modern Japanese spelling is analyzable as 空 (kara, “empty”) + 手 (te, “hand”). It replaced the earlier 唐手 (karate, “Chinese hand”), an orthographic borrowing from Okinawan 唐手 (tōdī, “Chinese hand”). During the early twentieth century, the first character was changed from 唐 (kara, “Tang dynasty; China”) to the homophonous 空 (kara, “empty”), while the pronunciation remained unchanged.

en.g: a diminutive of the male given name Johannes, from Dutch [in turn from Latin, in turn from Koine Greek, in turn from Biblical Hebrew] or from West Frisian [in turn from Latin, in turn from Koine Greek, in turn from Biblical Hebrew], equivalent to English John

1000218.etyen:
Borrowed from Dutch Jan (“male given name”) and West Frisian Jan (“male given name”) in the eighteenth century. Both are contracted forms corresponding to Johannes. The name ultimately derives from Latin Iohannes, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”). Doublet of Jon (“male given name”), the older traditional Norwegian form.
Compare Danish Jan, Swedish Jan, German Jan, Polish Jan and Czech Jan (“male given name”).

1004314.etyen:
Apparently a habitational surname from the farm name Berbu in Orkdal. The farm name is recorded with older spellings including Barbo, Barbou and Barboe. It is probably from Old Norse *Berubú, containing the river name *Bera and bú (“dwelling, farm”).
First attested in 1392 as Berabu and Bærabu.

weed harrowing; the act or process of controlling weeds mechanically with a weed harrow
x: Ugrasharving benyttes først og fremst i korn, erter, bønner, sukkerbeter, mais, potet og jordbær, men kan med forsiktighet også brukes i grønnsakdyrkingen.
Weed harrowing is used primarily in cereals, peas, beans, sugar beet, maize, potatoes and strawberries, but may also be used cautiously in vegetable cultivation.
Det må kalkuleres med en gang ugressharving og to ganger radrensing.
Provision should be made for one weed-harrowing pass and two rounds of inter-row cultivation.

1004826.etyen:
From ugressharve (“to control weeds with a weed harrow”) + -ing (“action/result-forming noun suffix”). The alternative spelling ugrasharving is attested in a 1954 source.
Parallel formations include Danish ukrudsharvning and Swedish ogräsharvning (“weed harrowing”).

1005082.etyen: Originally the genitive of faen (“the Devil”), later lexicalized as an indeclinable adjective.
